note: Both epd pages load and support 210 accused, 489 victims, study period 1941-2002, the 12 March 2026 publication, the city council's renaming and honorary-citizen decision, and 262 accused in the commission's fourth annual report. No changes.

fixes.d: A University of Passau team led by historian Marc von Knorring, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission, published its study online on 8 December 2025 covering 1945 to 2022. It found at least 672 minors, mostly boys, who were sexually abused or physically mistreated (or both) by 154 clergy, about 6.4% of some 2,400 priests, deacons and religious clergy in the period; 128 of them sexually abused minors, and about 86% were likely repeat offenders. Abuse took place in boarding schools and homes, religious lessons and altar-server duties. The study found bishops and vicars general often protected the institution and the priesthood rather than victims.

note: ZDFheute supports all figures and the publication on 8 December 2025; the 672 figure covers minors who were sexually abused or physically mistreated (or both), so d now says that.

fixes.d: Lawyer Hendrik Schneider, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission (UKAM), presented his report on 8 April 2025 covering 1949 to 2019. It counted 51 accused, 43 of them clergy, and 226 victims subject to 449 documented acts, which the report extrapolated to about 3,053 acts. The average age of victims at the first act was 9.8 years. It found systematic protection of some accused clergy until the early 2000s. Earlier, in 2019, lawyer Hans-Jochen Schrepfer reviewed nearly 3,000 personnel files, and the Würzburg law firm Cornea Franz reviewed the records of the diocese's three Kilianeen boys' boarding schools.
fixes.cite: Hendrik Schneider, report for the Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung des sexuellen Missbrauchs im Bistum Würzburg, 8 April 2025 (epd via evangelisch.de); epd, 19 November 2019, on the Schrepfer personnel-file review and the Kilianeen review

note: epd page supports 51 accused (43 clergy), 226 victims, 449 acts / 3,053 extrapolated, average age 9.8 and 'systematic protection' until the early 2000s. The last sentence on the 2019 reviews was not in that source; confirmed it from a second epd report (19 Nov 2019) and corrected who did the boarding-school review.

cite: Bistum Hildesheim, press kit for the presentation of the Niewisch-Lennartz/Schrimm/IPP report, 14 September 2021; epd via evangelisch.de, 14 September 2021

fixes.d: An external expert group led by former Lower Saxony justice minister Antje Niewisch-Lennartz, with former senior prosecutor Kurt Schrimm and the IPP institute, presented its report on 14 September 2021 on the tenure of Bishop Heinrich Maria Janssen (1957–1982). Its interviews identified 71 suspects, 45 of them clergy, the others lay staff, members of religious orders and youths in children's homes; 51 were active during Janssen's tenure. Accused priests were generally only transferred, in one case to South America, and children were left unprotected in tent camps, priests' homes and church children's homes. The group found no further evidence against Janssen himself but did not refute the two allegations made against him in 2015 and 2018. An earlier IPP study for the diocese appeared in 2017.

note: The diocese's own press kit for 14 Sept 2021 confirms 71 suspects, 45 of them clergy and 51 from Janssen's tenure, and lists the earlier IPP study (2017). The other 26 were lay staff, members of religious orders and youths in children's homes, not only lay staff, so d is corrected. epd's report gives a different count (81 suspects, 55 clergy); the press kit is used as the main source.

fixes.d: The diocese's independent review commission (UAKA) presented a 206-page study on 30 October 2025, built on the diocese's MHG-study data covering 1,507 personnel files of diocesan clergy. It found 77 accused linked to 193 offences against 156 victims, about two-thirds male and 42.5% under 14, with offences back to 1948. Diocesan leaders handled allegations inappropriately for decades, in up to 68.8% of cases under one bishop; handling improved after the 2002 guidelines. Bishop Bertram Meier said the diocese bore grave guilt.

note: Sonntagsblatt/epd supports the 30 October 2025 study, 206 pages, 1,507 files, 77 accused, 193 offences, 156 victims, the shares by bishop and the 2002 guidelines. The final sentence on the Heilig Kreuz and Reitenbuch home studies was not in the source and is removed.

fixes.d: The independent commission for the Diocese of Fulda, chaired by former Fulda mayor Gerhard Möller, presented its final report on 17 June 2025 after reviewing 2,124 files covering about 80 years. It identified 120 victims and 37 accused priests and chaplains, with 239 provable sexual offences, and said the true number is several times higher. Until about 2000 accused clergy were treated leniently and moved without explanation, and victims were ignored until 2010; auxiliary bishop Johannes Kapp, in charge of personnel from 1977 to 2003, was named as mainly responsible. Bishop Michael Gerber said the diocese had incurred guilt and church structures had failed.

note: epd supports 120 victims, 37 accused priests and chaplains, 239 provable offences, 2,124 files over 80 years, leniency until 2000, victims ignored until 2010 and Kapp's role. Bishop Gerber's words are corrected to what he said.

fixes.d: Historian Sylvia Schraut of the University of Mannheim, in a study begun in April 2023 at the initiative of the diocese's independent review commission, presented part 1 on 8 May 2025. It identified 109 accused clergy since 1946, two-thirds born before 1920; half the offences took place in the 1950s and 1960s, in church homes, lessons, confession and parish work. The church either punished accused priests individually or shielded them, and oversight of religious orders was weak. Part 2, with case analyses, is due in 2027. Separately, in 2020 the Darmstadt social court granted victim compensation to a man abused in the former Niederbronn Sisters' children's home in Speyer; he said the nuns brought children to abusers, and he and two other men independently said a former vicar general abused them there between 1963 and 1975.

note: Uni Mannheim release (8 May 2025) supports 109 accused, half the offences in the 1950s-60s, weak oversight of orders and part 2 due 2027. The epd 2020 report says the claimant said nuns delivered children to abusers and that he and two other men said a former vicar general abused them in 1963–1975; d is corrected to say this (the accused, who died in 1998, is not named).

fixes.d: The Diocese of Limburg ran a project with about 70 mostly external experts from September 2019 to June 2020 as its response to the 2018 MHG study; the 415-page final report was presented on 13 June 2020 in Frankfurt's Paulskirche. Its file review covered 46 cases and found that diocesan leaders had played down the crimes and treated the accused as a threat to the clerical system rather than a danger to children. It named the leaders responsible for cover-up and silence and produced 61 measures against abuse. Survivors who took part criticised how little affected people were involved.

note: Final report PDF and epd confirm 70 experts, the 415-page report presented on 13 June 2020 in the Paulskirche, 46 file cases, named responsibility for cover-up, the 'threat to the clerical system' finding and 61 measures. The last sentence is reworded to match what survivors said.

fixes.d: Forensic psychiatrists at the University of Ulm led by Manuela Dudeck, commissioned by the Archdiocese of Hamburg, presented their study in Schwerin on 24 February 2023. Reviewing 1,503 church and Stasi files, they identified 19 suspects and 40 victims; the 13 victims interviewed had been about 10 years old on average when the abuse began. Parishes and church leaders knew of abuse, and the study found a culture of silence and partly active cover-up. The Stasi recruited suspects as informers and used them, so prosecutions did not follow, and church–state arrangements such as moves to West Germany kept cases quiet.

note: epd supports the 24 Feb 2023 presentation, 1,503 church and Stasi files, 19 suspects, 40 victims, Stasi recruitment and moves to the West. The average age of about 10 refers to the 13 victims interviewed, so d is corrected.

The PDF URL returns 404 to a direct download, but the same document loaded through the fetch tool and confirms 23 February 2011, 120 complaints from 1950 into the 1980s, about half sexual and half physical, two-thirds clarified, and referral to prosecutors. No changes; the link may need replacing if it stays dead.

fixes.cover: Files of deceased friars appear to have been purged; before 2009 no sanctions against suspects were found; no church-law preliminary investigation was opened in any case, and the reviewers found no evidence that the province passed reports to prosecutors.
fixes.d: Lawyer Martin Pusch of Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the German Capuchin Province, reported on 30 November 2011. He found 32 accused friars, 19 of them accused of sexual abuse and at least 11 believed to have abused minors, mostly in schools and training institutions including the Burghausen seminary; no criminal or church-court conviction was found in any case. Files of deceased friars appeared to have been purged, and no sanctions were found before 2009, when three suspects were suspended and one elderly friar transferred. No church-law investigation was opened in any case, and before 2010 victims received no response or support.

note: Report PDF confirms 32 accused, 19 over sexual abuse, at least 11 with minor victims, mostly in schools, Burghausen, and files purged. It does not support 'quietly reassigned' or 'only one case reached prosecutors': it found no sanctions at all before 2009, one elderly friar transferred and three suspended after that, no sign that leaders passed reports to prosecutors, and no church-law investigation. cover and d are corrected.

epd (25 Sept 2026) supports the six interim reports, at least 90 victims and 29 perpetrators from 1950 to 2011, the Collegium Josephinum Bonn, and the 276-page IPP study with Heiner Keupp. No changes.

fixes.d: Lawyers Petra Ladenburger and Martina Lörsch presented a 152-page study on 10 June 2024, the first independent, externally overseen study of a Catholic order in Germany under the 2021 agreement between the orders' conference (DOK) and the federal abuse commissioner. It assessed allegations against nine friars since the 1960s; one friar was accused of abusing 20 people, and many victims were children in the order's boarding schools in Bonn and Würzburg. The committee overseeing the study said some accused abused for nearly 30 years before effective sanctions, because successive superiors did not enforce threatened consequences.

note: Vatican News supports the 10 June 2024 study, 152 pages, nine friars, one friar with 20 victims, boarding schools in Bonn and Würzburg, and the first study under the DOK agreement. The 30-year finding came from the advisory committee that oversaw the study; d is adjusted.

epd (25 Feb 2026) supports more than 100 victims, 98 suspects, 75% male, age 10–15, mostly in educational institutions, the provincial minister's admission of guilt, and the Vossenack survivor's accusation of cover-up. No changes.

epd supports the 15 Feb 2011 report, 58 reports against 23 staff (18 Jesuits, 5 lay), most active in the 1950s-60s, the ten cases against the former head who worked and lived there 1968–2008, the priest who was never stopped, and the comment on organisational culture. No changes.

The archdiocese press release (13 Sept 2017) supports about 100 former pupils, the 'system of abuse of power' up to at least the 1970s, seven accused of sexual violence (all but one priests), twelve of physical violence, and the lack of rules and oversight. y1 1979 is an approximation of 'at least into the 1970s'. No changes.

fixes.d: Bettina Janssen and Claudia Bundschuh presented their final report of about 140 pages on the diocesan boarding school Albertinum in Gerolstein on 11 February 2022, covering 1946 until it closed in 1983. Fifty-four former pupils came forward. Violence, mostly physical but including sexualised violence, was part of daily life; all three directors, who were priests, and one lay employee committed sexualised violence. Bishop Stephan Ackermann apologised and admitted the diocese had lacked effective oversight; by February 2023 the diocese had paid more than 650,000 euros to former pupils.

note: Both epd pages support the report, 54 former pupils, 1946–1983, sexualised violence by all three priest-directors and one lay worker, and Ackermann's apology. The payment was more than 650,000 euros.

epd supports the 7 June 2018 report, 115 interviews with 105 used, 56 reporting sexualised violence and 93 physical violence, the caretaker who abused at least 30 children, and payments usually of 5,000 euros. No changes.

fixes.victims_note: an estimated 11.4 million children (range 9.8–13.2 million) stayed in cure and recreation homes 1951–1990; the study says no count of mistreated children is possible
fixes.d: A Humboldt University team led by historian Alexander Nützenadel published the first nationwide report on West German children's cure homes on 15 May 2025, jointly with the German pension insurance (DRV), Caritas, Diakonie and the German Red Cross. It estimates that 11.4 million children stayed in such homes between 1951 and 1990 and describes humiliation, intimidation and violence as structural, caused by underfunding, staff shortages and inadequate supervision; many children faced physical, psychological and sexualised violence, though the study says no count is possible. No home was closed because of complaints. The four organisations expressed regret and accepted responsibility.

note: DRV press release (15 May 2025) and epd support the Humboldt study, 11.4 million children 1951–1990 (range 9.8–13.2 million), structural abuses and the four organisations' regret; epd says abuses included sexualised violence. The NRW 2022 study sentence was not in either source and is removed. In scope only partly: most findings concern non-sexual mistreatment.

fixes.d: The Göttingen Institute for Democracy Research led by Franz Walter, commissioned by the Greens, presented its report in November 2014: paedophile activists got demands to legalise sex between adults and children into several Green resolutions in the 1980s, until a clear break at federal level in 1989, while in the Berlin branch the debate continued into the mid-1990s. A Berlin state-party commission reported in May 2015. The party's working group was contacted by 12 victims of child sexual abuse; three received payments for long-term abuse in the early 1980s in the Christian Emmaus community at Dachsberg in Kamp-Lintfort, where the party's institutional co-responsibility could not be ruled out. The party apologised in November 2014.

note: The party's 2016 report supports the Göttingen study presented in November 2014, the 1989 break, the Berlin debate into the mid-1990s, the May 2015 Berlin commission, 12 victims who contacted the working group, and three payments for abuse in the Emmaus community at Dachsberg. 'Which ended in 2016' was not stated and is removed.

epd and the study PDF support the 24 Feb 2021 publication, authors Hax and Reiß, foster placements with paedosexual men, support from scientists, the Greens, child-rights groups and the left scene, opposition from the women's movement, Bahnhof Zoo and the call for a national inquiry. No changes.

epd supports the 24 May 2023 final report, Ziercke as chair, 52 of more than 80 suspected cases (2010–2014), the 2014 complaint and dismissal, the 2016 death, families informed only in 2019, and 5,000–50,000 euro payments. No changes.

fixes.d: The Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart's third report on investigation and recognition, with figures as of 1 September 2023 and published in October 2023, counted 207 accused (114 priests, deacons and male religious with a diocesan contract, 17 other religious priests, 54 lay people and 21 religious sisters) and 421 known victims for 1946 to 2023. Cases are handled by the diocese's abuse commission (KsM), set up in 2002. The diocese's independent review commission, formed in December 2021, published its first report in February 2023.
fixes.cite: Diözese Rottenburg-Stuttgart, 'Aufklärung, Aufarbeitung, Anerkennung des Leides, Prävention', 3rd edition, figures as of 1 September 2023 (press release 10 October 2023)

note: The PDF supports 207 accused with the stated breakdown, 421 victims, 1946 to 2023, KsM set up in 2002, and the first review-commission report in February 2023. Its figures are as of 1 September 2023 (third edition, press release 10 October 2023), not dated 19 October. The Josefsheim/IPP sentence was not in the source and is removed.

fixes.victims_note: by July 2015, 362 people in Tyrol had received compensation and 159 people in Vorarlberg had received financial support since 2010

note: University of Innsbruck page supports the 6 July 2015 presentation, the four homes, the 'total institution' finding and violence into the 1980s. Payments: 362 people in Tyrol; in Vorarlberg 159 people since 2010. victims_note adjusted.

fixes.d: A commission set up in 2019 by the State of Tyrol, the Diocese of Innsbruck and religious orders, chaired by Margret Aull, presented its final report 'Demut lernen' on 7 December 2022, written by historians Ina Friedmann and Friedrich Stepanek. Based on 75 interviews, it covered seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol after 1945, where former residents described structural, physical, psychological and sexualised violence; at Martinsbühel in the 1970s one sister looked after up to 50 girls. Survivors said state youth welfare and school authorities did not look closely enough. Bishop Hermann Glettler called the findings 'total pedagogical failure' in church and state institutions, and the state social affairs councillor apologised.
fixes.cite: Dreierkommission Martinsbühel, final report 'Demut lernen. Kindheit in konfessionellen Kinderheimen in Tirol nach 1945', 7 December 2022 (Amt der Tiroler Landesregierung press release)

note: The PDF is the Tyrol government's press release for the commission (7 Dec 2022), not the report itself; it supports the seven homes, 75 interviews, up to 50 girls per sister, sexualised violence and survivors' criticism of youth welfare. 'Total pedagogical failure' was said by Bishop Hermann Glettler; Aull's profession is not given. d and cite corrected.

Weisser Ring summary and profil (21 May 2012) support all figures: commissioned August 2010, 1945–1999, 3,139 reports, 2,384 people aided, 42.13 million euros, about 100,000 children, sadistic sexual abuse by some staff. No changes.

fixes.d: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.

note: The ISC summary report (6 June 2023) supports the chairs, the standard of proof, the abuse findings, cover-ups, failures to report, the named countries and the 991-page part two given to the Senate and Board on 2 May 2023. VOL.AT does not say Austrian prosecutors received parts; it says SOS International was still checking whether parts could be passed on. Last sentence corrected.

fixes.d: After a Falter report in September 2025 on abuse by staff at Austrian SOS children's villages, SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich said on 23 October 2025 that there were credible allegations that its founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986) sexually and physically abused eight boys at four villages between the 1950s and 1980s; victims had come forward from 2013 and received compensation and therapy, but the organisation had not made this public. A later investigation report listed 16 suspected cases of sexualised violence by Gmeiner. An external reform commission chaired by former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss presented its results on 25 June 2026, focusing on abuse at Moosburg and Imst, handling of earlier studies and possible cover-ups, and the lack of external oversight. Prosecutors in Klagenfurt, Innsbruck and Salzburg opened investigations.

note: Blue News (dpa, 23 Oct 2025), ORF (25 June 2026), VOL.AT and stol.it (26 June 2026, 16 suspected cases) support the record. The organisation called the allegations credible but they were never tested in court, so d now says 'credible allegations'.

fixes.d: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, published its 631-page report on 20 January 2025, described as the first fully independent study of its kind in Italy, covering 1964 to 2023. It found 29 clerics against whom allegations were proven or highly probable, in 67 cases of sexual assault with 59 victims, plus 16 unclear cases; one priest abused girls as young as seven and was removed only in 2010. It described the handling of cases until 2010 as a general and highly systemic failure. Bishop Ivo Muser said 'every case is one too many' and that victims' suffering should fill the church with shame.

note: Politiko/BishopAccountability supports 20 Jan 2025, 1964–2023, 29 clerics, 67 cases, 59 victims plus 16 unclear, 51% female, 'systemic failure' until 2010 and the priest removed in 2010. The source does not report an apology; it quotes the bishop on shame. The Avvenire url2 returns 404 and is removed.

Il Post (17 Nov 2022) and Sky TG24 (28 May 2025) support all figures: 86 contacts, 89 people, 68 alleged abusers 44% clergy, 613 files to the Vatican, and 115 alleged victims (64 boys, 51 girls) with 67 alleged perpetrators (44 clergy) in 2023–2024; also the critics. No changes.

fixes.d: In January 2021 the Jesuits in Spain published a report admitting 118 cases of sexual abuse since 1927, 81 of them against children and 37 against adults. It named 96 accused Jesuits, about 1.08% of members since 1927; of the 65 who abused children, 48 had died and 17 were alive. AP described it as the first comprehensive internal inquiry into abuse by a religious order in Spain. Victims' groups criticised it for not naming perpetrators or those who covered up abuse.
fixes.cite: Compañía de Jesús en España, report on abuse cases since 1927, January 2021 (JURIST, January 2021; AP, Aritz Parra and Nicole Winfield, 22 January 2021)

note: JURIST blocks direct download but loaded through the fetch tool; it supports 118 cases, 81 children, 37 adults, 96 Jesuits, 1.08%, 65 who abused children (48 dead, 17 alive). AP (22 Jan 2021) calls it the first comprehensive internal inquiry by a religious order in Spain. Neither source says the order admitted mishandling; that sentence is replaced with victims' groups' criticism from AP.

fixes.cite: Hermanos Maristas, announcement of 3 December 2020 (AFP via Semanario Universidad)

note: Semanario Universidad supports 25 victims recognised on 3 Dec 2020, about 400,000 euros, the 2016 press revelations about Barcelona schools 1970–2010, and Joaquín Benítez's 2019 sentence of 21 years nine months (convicted, so naming is allowed). The agency is AFP, not EFE. first_report 2016 is the press exposure, not a documented first complaint, so it is cleared.

betevé (2 Oct 2020) supports the ombudsman's report findings (boys 5–17, 1960s–70s, three 1990s cases, camps and church premises, many more victims, congregations not proactive, seven recommendations); elDiario.es confirms the Parliament inquiry approved 27 April 2022. No changes.

fixes.d: A commission of the Consell de Mallorca, chaired by vice-president Jaume Tortella, reported on 23 April 2021 on the sexual exploitation of minors in the care of the island's child-protection agency IMAS; about 16 cases were known in January 2020, 13 of them from 2017 to early 2019. With the PP and Vox refusing to take part, it found no political, technical or criminal responsibility and no network linking the cases, matching the prosecutors' investigation. Reporting had changed in February 2020 so that suspicions go to the national police, and five cases not previously reported were sent to prosecutors. In late 2020 two men were convicted of corrupting girls in care, and in April 2022 a European Parliament Petitions Committee delegation visited Palma to examine the cases.

note: Ultima Hora (23 April 2021) supports the commission's findings, the about 16 cases (13 from 2017 to early 2019), the February 2020 reporting change and five cases sent to prosecutors. The April 2022 visit was by a European Parliament Petitions Committee delegation; PP and Vox refused to join the commission, saying its conclusions were predetermined. d adjusted.

fixes.d: The federal Chamber set up a parliamentary commission of inquiry into sexual abuse in the Church and elsewhere, chaired by Sophie De Wit (N-VA), after the 2023 VRT series 'Godvergeten'. Its final report of 2 May 2024 made 137 recommendations, including that the Church proactively trace perpetrators through its archives and give police and courts access to relevant church files, and a legal study on retroactively ending the limitation period for child sexual abuse. It called for reducing the 58% of sexual-violence cases dismissed by prosecutors, and for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' investigation after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions. It proposed an abuse commissioner, a centre of expertise and an arbitration body for time-barred cases.

note: VRT NWS (2 May 2024) supports the 137 recommendations, the commissioner, expertise centre, arbitration body, study of ending limitation retroactively, archive searches and police access to church files, the 58% dismissal figure and the call for a new Kelk inquiry. It does not mention a call for the Church to 'acknowledge responsibility', so that is removed; the 58% concerns sexual-violence files generally.

rkkerk.nl supports 11 March 2013, 1945–2012, the 77% male finding of 2011, 79 new reports (37 without sexual abuse), 71 earlier reports reconsidered (26 from women), and the call to bishops and superiors. No changes.

fixes.d: An independent working group formed at the request of the abbey, then under a Vatican-appointed apostolic administrator, by Neuchâtel attorney general Pierre Aubert presented its findings on 20 June 2025. Historians of the University of Fribourg (Anne-Françoise Praz, Stéphanie Roulin and others) and retired judge Claire-Lise Mayor Aubert heard about 50 witnesses and 24 clergy and examined sexual violence at the abbey and its boarding school from 1960 to 2024. They found sexualised touching by canons, ambiguous photo sessions, exhibitionism and use of child abuse material; since 1970 five criminal penalty orders had been issued against three canons and a novice, and members with ambiguous or unlawful conduct were left in office without precautions. The mandate did not cover the abbey's collège.

note: Uni Fribourg page and SRF support the 20 June 2025 report, the team, 1960–2024 and the exclusion of the collège. d now adds SRF's main findings (about 50 witnesses and 24 clergy heard; five criminal penalty orders against three canons and a novice since 1970; members with unlawful conduct left in office).

Blitz Quotidiano (ANSA-based) supports 45 cases since 1991, 19 unfounded, 13 open, four priests found guilty by the Holy See and removed, two dead, and Judge Caruana Colombo as head. No changes; a Maltese outlet would be a stronger source if one is found.
The Pillar via BishopAccountability supports the Evaluation Report 2018–2023, complaints since 1990, 68/39/17/7/5, more than 44 victims, 50 Latin, 3 Greek Catholic and 15 order cases. No changes.

cite: The Baltic Times, 'Two child abusers get sentences, others line up', 19 October 2000; Wikipedia, 'Logos Centrs pedophilia case', citing Latvijas Vēstnesis (2000) and Delfi

fixes.d: After a September 1999 Latvian TV report, prosecutors investigated the Riga agency Logos Centrs, headed by Jurijs Jurjevs, which The Baltic Times described as a bogus modelling agency running a child pornography and prostitution ring; seven people were charged. Andris Meinarts was convicted on 21 counts of sexually abusing minors as a customer and sentenced to ten years, the maximum; pageant agency manager Ainārs Eisaks received 2.5 years; Ingus Tūns' case was tried separately. According to Wikipedia, citing Latvijas Vēstnesis and Delfi, 67 people, 61 of them minors, were sexually exploited, the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors, Jurjevs received more than four years and Tūns five. Claims that senior politicians were clients were investigated and found false (see the Saeima commission record).
fixes.victims_note: 67 people sexually exploited, 61 of them minors; the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors (figures from Wikipedia citing Latvijas Vēstnesis, not independently confirmed)

note: Wikipedia carries a May 2026 warning that it may contain LLM-written text, so the main url is changed to The Baltic Times (19 Oct 2000), which confirms Meinarts' 10 years on 21 counts, Eisaks' 2.5 years, Tūns' separate case and the September 1999 TV report. The 67/61/3,000 figures, Jurjevs' sentence of over four years and Tūns' five years appear only in Wikipedia (citing Latvijas Vēstnesis and Delfi), which I could not open; they are kept but marked as Wikipedia-based. Uncertain.

fixes.d: After a September 1999 TV report on the Logos Centrs case, the Saeima set up an investigation commission chaired by opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons, who on 17 February 2000 publicly linked former prime minister Andris Šķēle, former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and revenue service head Andrejs Sončiks to the paedophilia case. On 1 August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the cases against them, stating it was 'fully proved' that the information given to the commission about them was false. Ādamsons was later convicted of slander; in February 2007 the Supreme Court upheld a fine of 10,400 lats. None of the officials was charged.
fixes.cite: Prosecutor General's Office of Latvia, decision of 1 August 2000 (The Baltic Times, 3 August 2000); The Baltic Times, 'Court upholds verdict against Adamsons', 21 February 2007

note: The Baltic Times (3 Aug 2000) confirms the 1 August 2000 closure and the 'fully proved' false-information wording for Šķēle, Birkavs and Sončiks. The Baltic Times (21 Feb 2007) shows Ādamsons was convicted of slander (Supreme Court upheld, fine 10,400 lats), not abuse of office as Wikipedia says; d corrected.

fixes.victims_note: 349 identifiable victims and firm indications of at least 60 more (more than 400) from 1945 to 2024; the study says the hidden number may be up to ten times higher
fixes.n: Germany — Diocese of Osnabrück, University of Osnabrück study (interim report 2022, final report 2024)
fixes.d: Historians and lawyers at the University of Osnabrück led by Hans Schulte-Nölke and Siegrid Westphal, commissioned by the diocese, presented a roughly 600-page interim report on 20 September 2022 on sexual violence by clergy since 1945; it criticised the handling of allegations under Bishop Franz-Josef Bode (from 1995) and his predecessors, finding he repeatedly left accused priests in office and assigned some to posts that enabled further abuse. Bode accepted responsibility and resigned in 2023. The final report, presented on 2 October 2024, named 122 accused clerics, about 4% of priests who served in the diocese since 1945 (an area that until 1995 included today's Archdiocese of Hamburg), and 349 identifiable victims with firm indications of at least 60 more; the study says the hidden number may be up to ten times higher.
fixes.cite: University of Osnabrück (Schulte-Nölke, Westphal et al.), interim report, 20 September 2022 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability) and final report, 2 October 2024 (statement of Vicar General Ulrich Beckwermert, 9 October 2024; Vatican News, 9 October 2024)

note: Confirmed: the University of Osnabrück presented its final report on Wednesday 2 October 2024 (the vicar general's statement of 9 October says 'last Wednesday'; Vatican News 9 Oct 2024). It names 122 accused clerics (priests and deacons, about 4% of priests since 1945) and 349 identifiable victims plus firm indications of at least 60 more, i.e. more than 400; the hidden number may be up to ten times higher. The area until 1995 included today's Archdiocese of Hamburg. The interim-report facts and the leaders Schulte-Nölke and Westphal check out (BishopAccountability, epd 2022). Bode's March 2023 resignation is supported as '2023' by Vatican News.
